query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, exposure to oxidizing or reducing gas environments promotes selective grain boundary oxidation and/or the precipitation of embrittling, brittle phases (e.g., Cr-/Al-rich oxides) within the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy. This localized degradation along grain boundaries weakens intergranular cohesion and triggers catastrophic intergranular cracking under load.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy featuring an FCC matrix with as-built grain boundary features and minimal pre-existing oxidation or embrittling second phases.
generation.intervention: Conduct a controlled thermal exposure study where samples are separately exposed to a high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing environment) and a hydrogen-rich or low oxygen environment (reducing conditions) at high temperatures.
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures within the 700–1050 °C range for durations up to 100 hours; gas compositions are precisely controlled to toggle between oxidizing and reducing regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of oxide scales or embrittling precipitates localized at grain boundaries, which act as stress concentrators and weaken intergranular bonding.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced diffusion at high temperatures leads to selective oxidation and/or phase separation along the grain boundaries. Under oxidizing conditions, elements like Cr and Al preferentially form brittle oxide precipitates that compromise grain boundary integrity, while reducing conditions may slow or alter this process. The loss in cohesion causes an earlier onset of intergranular cracking and catastrophic failure when mechanical stress is applied.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the starting-state baseline, samples exposed to an oxidizing environment will exhibit thicker, more continuous grain boundary oxide layers and a higher density of brittle, embrittling phases, leading to reduced ductility and lower fracture toughness. In contrast, samples under reducing conditions should show less pronounced grain boundary degradation and better retention of mechanical properties, delaying catastrophic failure.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated alloy state with minimal grain boundary oxidation or embrittling phase formation, where the material retains its designed high strength and ductility.
generation.boundary: The temperature range must be high enough (above approximately 700 °C) to activate significant diffusion and oxidation kinetics, yet below temperatures (>1050 °C) where general oxidation may dominate and obscure grain-boundary–focused effects.
generation.uncertainty: The exact balance between oxygen-driven oxidation kinetics and the intrinsic effects of the additively manufactured microstructure (including any residual stresses or grain boundary heterogeneity) on embrittlement remains uncertain. Additionally, the relative contribution of each element’s diffusion (e.g., Cr vs. Al) to the formation of harmful phases under different gas chemistries is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the alloy and expose them for 100 hours at a fixed elevated temperature (e.g., 900 °C) in two environments: one under high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing) and the other under a reducing atmosphere (e.g., H2-rich or low O2). Following exposure, perform mechanical tests (tensile or fracture toughness) and microstructural analyses (TEM/SEM, XRD) to assess grain boundary oxidation, phase precipitation, and fracture modes.
measurements: Grain boundary oxide/precipitate thickness and distribution (via TEM/SEM)
Phase identification of any secondary/brittle phases using XRD
Mechanical properties: ductility, fracture toughness, and stress at failure
Fractography to confirm intergranular crack paths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference in grain boundary oxidation, embrittling phase formation, or corresponding mechanical degradation is observed between the oxidizing and reducing conditions compared to the baseline, or if intergranular cracking is not the dominant failure mode in the oxidized samples, then the hypothesis that degradation is governed by selective grain boundary oxidation/embrittlement is falsified.

The classical “temper embrittlement” phenomenon [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] —documented for over a century in conventional steels and other alloys—occurs upon exposure to specific temperature ranges, sharply reducing toughness and endangering engineering safety in critical applications such as aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical systems. [ [8] , [9] , [10] ] Temper embrittlement degradation is primarily attributed to the segregation of embrittling elements or the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries (GBs), which act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, ultimately inducing brittle fracture under stress. [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [7] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ] This well‐established mechanism highlights the central role of brittle phase precipitation and element segregation at GBs in governing embrittlement in conventional alloys.

Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
